chunks: Muhammad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn al-Husayn, from Safwan, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, who said:

I asked him about currency exchange (as-sarf). I said to him: 'The caravan/group sometimes hurries and departs, so we are unable to obtain the Damascus dirhams and the Basran dirhams, and instead it is permissible with a Sabur [a specific weight/measure] of the Damascus and Basran [coins].' He said: 'And what is the Rifqa (caravan/group)?' I said: 'The people associate with one another and gather for departure. So when they hurry, and sometimes we are unable to obtain the Damascus and Basran [dirhams], we send with the proceeds [proceeds of sale], and they exchange one thousand and fifty dirhams from it with one thousand from the Damascus and Basran [dirhams].' He said: 'There is no goodness in this. Why do you not place gold in it due to its increase [in value/weight]?'

I said to him: 'Can I buy one thousand dirhams and one dinar with two thousand dirhams?' He said: 'There is no problem with that. Indeed, my father (peace be upon him) used to be more accommodating with the people of Medina than I was, and he used to say this. So they would say: 'This is merely fleeing [from the strict rule]. If a man came with one dinar, he would not be given one thousand dirhams, and if he came with one thousand dirhams, he would not be given one thousand dinars.' And he used to say to them: 'Excellent is the fleeing from the forbidden to the permissible.'
Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, and Muhammad ibn Ismail, from al-Fadl ibn Shadhan, from Safwan ibn Yahya and Ibn Abi Umeyr, from Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Hajjaj, similar to it.

key_terms.الدِّمَشْقِيَّة: Damascus dirhams (a type of silver coin)
key_terms.الْبَصْرِيَّة: Basran dirhams (a type of silver coin)
key_terms.الْفِرَار: Fleeing (metaphor for avoiding strict equality to prevent invalidity)
key_terms.سَابُور: A specific weight or measure of coins

ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on exchanging silver for gold with a slight difference in amount to avoid hardship?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi elucidates the Shia juristic principle of 'al-firar min al-haram ila al-halal' (fleeing from the forbidden to the permissible), where a slight excess in currency exchange is permitted to avoid the strict equality required in riba-free transactions, thereby preventing invalidity due to delay or hardship. Imam al-Sadiq (AS) cites his father, Imam al-Baqir (AS), who routinely allowed such flexibility among the people of Medina, demonstrating a pragmatic approach to commercial law that prioritizes the validity of the contract over rigid formalism. This reflects the broader Shia methodology of using 'urf' (customary practice) and ease to facilitate trade while maintaining the core prohibition of usury.
